Chemical structure and biosynthesis of itaconate

Chemical structure and biosynthesis of itaconate. A: Itaconate is an endogenous metabolite produced in activated macrophages through the decarboxylation of cis-aconitate, a tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediate. This reaction is catalyzed by ACOD1, also known as IRG1, localized in the mitochondrial matrix. Once synthesized, itaconate can undergo further metabolic transformation into itaconyl-CoA via CoA ligation, and subsequently into (S)-citramalyl-CoA, linking it to broader mitochondrial metabolic circuits. In vivo, itaconate is eliminated through urinary excretion and further metabolized into acetyl-CoA, mesaconate, and citramalate. B: Various pattern recognition receptors and cytokine signaling pathways jointly regulate the transcription of ACOD1.ACOD1: Aconitate decarboxylase 1; BoNT/A: Botulinum neurotoxin serotype A; BRD3: Bromodomain-containing protein 3; CDK2: Cyclin-dependent kinase 2; CpG: Cytosine–phosphate–Guanine oligodeoxynucleotide; CREB1: cAMP response element-binding protein 1; CREBBP: CREB-binding protein; DRD2: Dopamine receptor D2; IRF3: Interferon regulatory factor 3; IRG1: Immune-responsive gene 1; JUN: Jun proto-oncogene, AP-1 transcription factor subunit; LTA: Lipoteichoic acid; LPS: Lipopolysaccharide; MAPK8/ JNK1: Mitogen-activated protein kinase 8; MYD88: Myeloid differentiation primary response 88; RACK1: Receptor for activated C kinase 1; STING1: Stimulator of interferon response cGAMP interactor 1; TCA: Tricarboxylic acid; TRIM21: Tripartite motif-containing protein 21; TLR: Toll-like receptors
